title: The Canon Formation Argument

keyTerms.d: “Canon” comes from the Greek kanōn, a measuring reed or rule — a standard. To speak of the biblical canon is to speak of the list of books the church received as the rule of its faith.

The canon was not decided at a moment; it emerged over centuries. The better way to describe what the church did is not that it created a canon but that it gradually recognized one — sifting the writings already circulating under its hand, testing them against criteria, and slowly arriving at a list.

Apostolicity, the first and most important: did the writing come from an apostle or a close associate of one? Orthodoxy, the “rule of faith”: was the book consonant with the teaching the churches had received? Catholicity, or widespread use: was it received and read across the scattered churches, not just prized by one faction in one region?

A short summary of the apostolic preaching, handed down in the churches and attested independently of any list: Irenaeus sets it out around AD 180, and a little later Tertullian names it the regula fidei. These summaries do not name which books belong in the canon.

In the early fourth century — and crucially, before Nicaea — Eusebius sorts the writings into the “recognized” (homologoumena), the “disputed” (antilegomena), and the “spurious” (notha). A careful sorting by inherited usage was already underway before Constantine’s council met.

An anonymous list that names most of the books we know — the oldest surviving canon list. It is mutilated at both ends, accepts the Wisdom of Solomon and, with hesitation, the Apocalypse of Peter, and omits Hebrews, James, and 1–2 Peter. Its date is debated: late-second-century (roughly AD 170–200) is the majority view; a minority argues for the fourth century.

Athanasius’s Easter letter of 367 is the first surviving list that matches our twenty-seven New Testament books exactly; he calls them “fountains of salvation.” He writes as one recording a settled deposit, not legislating a new one.

Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include a set of Old Testament books and additions — Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1 and 2 Maccabees, and parts of Daniel and Esther — that they call deuterocanonical (“second canon”) and that Protestants call the Apocrypha and place outside the canon (Orthodox canons are broader still). Both traditions can point to early precedent; it is a real and reasonable disagreement that this argument does not adjudicate.

derive.q: Eusebius sorts the books into recognized, disputed and spurious before Nicaea ever meets — so the council…?
derive.ans: did not create the canon; the sorting already existed
derive.why: The Council of Nicaea did not vote on the canon, did not discuss the canon, and left no record of anyone raising the subject; its business was the relationship of Christ to the Father in the Arian controversy. Eusebius’s snapshot is the decisive evidence against the conspiracy story: a careful sorting by inherited usage was already underway before Constantine’s council met.

derive.q: Around AD 180 Irenaeus treats any number of Gospels other than four as self-evidently absurd — so by then…?
derive.ans: a fourfold Gospel was already an established fact
derive.why: His comparison of the Gospels to the four zones of the world and the four winds is a strange-sounding argument to modern ears, but it only works if a fourfold Gospel was already an established fact his readers would not dispute. Irenaeus is the earliest surviving witness to treat all four canonical Gospels as a fixed and necessary set.

derive.q: The canonical four date to the first century; Thomas, Peter and Judas, as we have them, to the second or later — so the rival gospels were excluded…?
derive.ans: rightly set aside: as we have them, too late to be apostolic
derive.why: The decisive point is chronology, not theology. These works were written generations after the apostles whose names they borrow, and often betray that lateness in their developed Gnostic theology. The exclusion was not, at root, the silencing of equally ancient witnesses; it was the recognition that the late pseudonymous works were exactly that.

derive.q: The church kept Revelation, Hebrews and 2 Peter through long doubt — so its criteria…?
derive.ans: had teeth; the process was not results-driven
derive.why: The church kept books it would have found convenient to drop: Revelation was doubted by serious orthodox figures for centuries yet retained; Hebrews was kept despite its anonymity; 2 Peter survived a long shadow of doubt. A purely results-driven process would have been tidier than the messy, hesitant one the sources actually record.

derive.q: The rule of faith is attested around AD 180 and names no books — so the orthodoxy criterion…?
derive.ans: was not reverse-engineered from a list of books
derive.why: The rule of faith was a short summary of the apostolic preaching, attested independently of any list, so the standard did not depend on the list. That answers one form of the circularity charge; it does not prove the criterion infallible, and it does not by itself show that the summary faithfully preserves what the apostles taught — that is a further historical question.

honestState.p1: Among historians who actually work on the canon, the broad outline is not seriously contested, and it crosses the ideological spectrum: the core books were received early, no ecumenical council “created” the canon, Nicaea did not address it, and the process was one of gradual recognition extending over centuries. Even Bart Ehrman affirms the basic chronology and rejects the Constantine myth. The live debates are more refined: how early the four-Gospel collection truly crystallized; whether the Muratorian Fragment is late-second-century (the majority view, defended by scholars like Joseph Verheyden) or fourth-century (a minority view argued by Geoffrey Hahneman and Albert Sundberg); how much weight to give “intrinsic” versus “community” factors in explaining reception; how to characterize the diversity of earliest Christianity; and whether Thomas preserves an early independent core (Mark Goodacre and Simon Gathercole argue it knows the Synoptics; April DeConick and Stephen Patterson defend an early and independent core). These are disagreements about the mechanism and timing of recognition, not about whether the canon was voted into being by an emperor.
honestState.fairness: The factual kernel of Ehrman’s objection is accurate, and an honest apologist should grant it: the early Jesus movement was more diverse than the tidy Sunday-school picture suggests, there really were competing groups with competing texts, and the proto-orthodox did prevail. The doubts over the disputed books were not trivial or quickly resolved — in some regions they persisted into the fifth century and beyond. And the church’s judgments about authorship were made with the limited tools of antiquity and are regarded as insecure by many modern critics, though those judgments are themselves contested by other scholars, evangelical and Catholic. What does not follow is the inference that prevailing is all that orthodoxy was: diversity at the start is fully compatible with a principled sorting later, and the argument requires only that the canon was formed by a discriminating reception keyed to perceived apostolic connection and widespread use — which is true whether or not every individual judgment about authorship would survive a modern seminar.
honestState.verdict: The canon was not handed down by Constantine, not voted on at Nicaea, and not imposed by a late council on a church that had no Bible until then. The core of the New Testament was received as Scripture within the first and second centuries, sifted by criteria of apostolic origin, orthodoxy, and widespread use, and only formally ratified once a consensus had long existed. The disputed books were genuinely disputed — evidence of care, not of fabrication — and the differences that remain among Christians concern the extent of the Old Testament, not the New Testament, a disagreement this argument does not adjudicate. The conspiracy story collapses under the weight of the actual sources. But showing that the church recognized these books does not, by itself, show that they are inspired or true; that is a further question, argued on further grounds — and, decisively, whether Jesus rose from the dead. Recognizing the canon is where the conversation about its truth can honestly begin — not where it ends.

order: If the church recognized writings that already carried authority, rather than conferring it by vote, the canon reflects something found, not manufactured.
The historical evidence shows the core books were received and used as authoritative long before any council ratified a list.
Therefore the canon is a recognition of books the churches already received as authoritative, not a late ecclesiastical invention.

props.t: the core books were received as Scripture long before any council ratified a list
the Council of Nicaea never took up the canon

the criteria had teeth: the church kept books it would have found convenient to drop

the Muratorian Fragment’s second-century date is undisputed

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and what it does NOT claim.
cards.a: If the church recognized writings that already carried authority, rather than creating their authority by vote, then the canon reflects something the church found rather than something it manufactured. It does not claim that recognition proves the contents inspired — that is a different argument, resting on different grounds.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and where the disputes actually clustered.
cards.a: The core books were received, copied, and cited as Scripture long before any council ratified a list. The disputes clustered at the edges: a handful of shorter or later-attested books were contested, while the four Gospels, Acts, and the letters of Paul — the doctrinal core — were never seriously in question.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the canon is recognition, not invention: it dismantles the conspiracy story and shows the canon to be the fruit of a discriminating, centuries-long reception rather than a fourth-century political fiat. It does not, by itself, show that the books are inspired or true; that is argued on further grounds.

cards.q: What was the Council of Nicaea’s actual business — and what did Constantine select?
cards.a: The relationship of Christ to the Father in the Arian controversy; it did not vote on, discuss, or record anyone raising the canon. Constantine selected nothing: the four-Gospel core was already functioning as Scripture generations before he was born.

cards.q: Why is the early-fourth-century sorting into “recognized,” “disputed,” and “spurious” books decisive?
cards.a: Because it comes before Nicaea: a careful sorting by inherited usage was already underway before Constantine’s council met. That is the decisive evidence against the conspiracy story.

cards.q: Why does Irenaeus’s “four winds” argument for exactly four Gospels count as evidence?
cards.a: It is a strange-sounding argument to modern ears, but it only works if, around AD 180, a fourfold Gospel was already an established fact his readers would not dispute.

cards.q: The oldest surviving canon list — what does it show, and how secure is its date?
cards.a: It already looks substantially like the New Testament, though it is mutilated at both ends, accepts the Wisdom of Solomon, and omits Hebrews, James, and 1–2 Peter. Its date is debated: late second century is the majority view; a minority argues for the fourth century.

cards.q: What did the 367 Easter list and the councils of Hippo and Carthage actually do?
cards.a: The Easter list records a settled deposit of New Testament books rather than legislating a new one. The regional councils listed and affirmed the canon for North Africa when the New Testament core had been read as Scripture for the better part of three centuries: they did not vote books into existence; they ratified a consensus long since reached. (Their lists also included the books Catholics and Orthodox call deuterocanonical, which Athanasius set apart as books to be read — a real, reasonable disagreement this argument does not adjudicate.)

cards.q: Why were the Gospels of Thomas, Peter, and Judas left out?
cards.a: Chronology, not theology, is the decisive point: as we have them they are second-century or later, written generations after the apostles whose names they borrow, so they failed the test of apostolic origin on historical grounds. The four canonical Gospels date to the first century, within living memory of the events. Ancient judges also weighed doctrine (Serapion’s verdict on the Gospel of Peter was partly doctrinal), but his stated ground was also provenance, a book “not handed down to us.”

cards.q: Is the Gospel of Thomas an early, independent rival to the four?
cards.a: Genuinely contested: a strong line of scholarship argues it draws on the finished Synoptics, while others defend an early and independent core. But even on the more cautious readings, Thomas as we have it is a second-century Greek composition that stands downstream of the first-century Gospels, not a first-century rival to them.

cards.q: Reply to: “The orthodoxy test is circular — they kept the books that already agreed with them.”
cards.a: The rule of faith was not drawn up to fit a list: it is a short summary of the apostolic preaching, attested around AD 180 independently of any list, and it names no books. And the criteria had teeth — the church kept Revelation, Hebrews, and 2 Peter through long doubt. This does not prove the criterion infallible; it shows the criterion did not decide the outcome.

cards.q: Why do Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant Bibles differ — and what does that do to the argument?
cards.a: The difference lies in the extent of the Old Testament — the books Catholics and Orthodox call deuterocanonical and Protestants call the Apocrypha; both traditions can point to early precedent, and the argument does not adjudicate it. On the twenty-seven-book New Testament all three are unanimous, so the disagreement leaves the New Testament canon, and the conspiracy-theory framing, untouched.

obj.q: Earliest Christianity was a roiling diversity — Ebionites, Marcionites, Gnostics — each with its own gospels and each claiming apostolic pedigree. As Bart Ehrman argues, “orthodoxy” was simply the party that won: the canon is history written by the winners. On this telling, Thomas, Peter, Mary and Judas were silenced not because they were demonstrably late but because they lost a power struggle.
obj.model: The factual kernel is accurate, and it should be granted: the early Jesus movement was more diverse than the tidy Sunday-school picture suggests, there really were competing groups with competing texts, and the proto-orthodox did prevail. What does not follow is the inference that prevailing is all that orthodoxy was. The decisive point is chronology, not theology: the canonical four date to the first century, within living memory of the events, while the Gospel of Thomas as we have it, the Gospel of Peter, the Gospel of Judas, and the rest are second-century or later — Judas, published in 2006, is a Sethian Gnostic text generally dated to around the mid-second century, far too late to come from Judas. Whether Thomas preserves an early independent core is contested, but even on the more cautious readings it stands downstream of the first-century Gospels. These works failed the test of apostolic origin on historical grounds, and the four were already being received across the churches before most of these rivals were even composed. So the “history written by the winners” objection does not hold: the Gospels the church kept are the first-century ones, and the rival gospels it set aside are, as we have them, second-century or later.

obj.q: Your orthodoxy criterion is circular. A book counted as orthodox if it agreed with the views of the group doing the judging, so “testing against the rule of faith” just means “keeping the books that already agree with us.” The “criteria” look less like neutral tests and more like rationalizations for choices made on other grounds.
obj.model: Grant the possibility of abuse: “agrees with the rule of faith” could in principle be used to launder a predetermined result. But the rule of faith was not drawn up to fit a list of books. It was a short summary of the apostolic preaching, attested independently of any list: around AD 180 Irenaeus sets it out as the faith the church “has received from the apostles and their disciples,” held by believers “without paper or ink,” and a little later Tertullian names it the regula fidei — and these summaries do not name which books belong in the canon. That answers one form of the charge — that the criterion was reverse-engineered from a predetermined list. It does not answer the deeper form — that the rule itself was simply the winning party’s view; that is met on chronology, since the rival gospels are, as we have them, second-century or later. Nor does it prove the criterion infallible, or by itself show that the summary faithfully preserves what the apostles taught. And in practice the criteria constrained one another: apostolicity and catholicity ask when a book was written and where it was received, and the proof that the criteria had teeth is that the church kept books it would have found convenient to drop — Revelation, Hebrews, 2 Peter. A purely results-driven process would have been tidier than the messy, hesitant one the sources actually record. So the circularity charge does not hold as an account of the outcome: the criterion did not decide it.

obj.q: You keep appealing to “apostolic origin,” but several of your own canonical books are pseudonymous by the judgment of most critical scholars — the Pastoral Epistles, 2 Peter, perhaps Ephesians. As Bart Ehrman presses it, the church enforced a criterion it could not actually verify, and sometimes got it wrong.
obj.model: That is the objection at its sharpest, and it must be acknowledged: the church’s judgments about authorship were made with the limited tools of antiquity and are regarded as insecure by many modern critics — though those judgments are themselves contested by other scholars, evangelical and Catholic, The reply is bounded but real. Even granting disputed authorship for a few books, the argument does not require that every canonical attribution be correct. It requires that the canon was formed by a discriminating reception keyed to perceived apostolic connection and widespread use — and that is true whether or not every individual judgment about authorship would survive a modern seminar. So the objection does not overturn the argument: the process was principled even on the critics’ own assumptions about authorship.

obj.q: If the canon were obvious, why did Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude and Revelation stay in doubt for generations — in some regions into the fifth century? Prolonged uncertainty looks like a list that was negotiated, not found.
obj.model: The doubts were real, and it would be dishonest to pretend they were trivial: Hebrews was questioned in the West because its authorship was uncertain; James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, and Jude were received slowly and unevenly — 2 Peter is the most weakly attested book in the New Testament in the early centuries; Revelation was doubted for a long time in the Greek East; and in some regions the doubts persisted into the fifth century and beyond. But the very existence of a category of “disputed” books shows the church was not rubber-stamping; it was sifting, sometimes for generations, before settling — what careful recognition looks like, not what a coordinated invention looks like. The disputes clustered at the edges: the four Gospels, Acts, and the letters of Paul were never seriously in question, and none of the disputed books carries a central doctrine the rest of the New Testament does not teach independently. So the prolonged doubt is not evidence of invention: a stable, early core and a slowly resolved fringe is the signature of discovery, not decree.

unseen.q: Fine — grant your history: no vote at Nicaea, an early core, careful criteria. But a careful, centuries-long reception is just what you would get if these were merely the earliest and best-attested human documents of a new religion. A church recognizing a book does not make it the word of God.
unseen.model: Grant what is true in it: showing that the church recognized these books does not, by itself, show that they are inspired or true, and a discriminating, principled, centuries-long reception is — as a skeptic may insist — compatible with their being merely the earliest and best-attested human documents of a new religion. But the canon argument never claimed more. It is also exactly what we would expect if these were the genuine apostolic writings, and what the historical argument does is clear the ground: it removes the charge that the Bible is a fourth-century political invention and shows the canon to be a thoughtful inheritance. Whether the books it preserves are the word of God is a further question, argued on further grounds — how early and how close to the events the Gospels stand, whether the Scriptures cohere as the unified testimony they claim to be, and, decisively, whether Jesus rose from the dead. So the objection does not defeat the canon argument; it names the next question. Recognizing the canon is where the conversation about its truth can honestly begin — not where it ends.
